title: Airbnb’s CEO says nobody builds AI for normal people. He is on Y Combinator’s board
excerpt: Brian Chesky says the consumer AI gap is why Americans dislike AI. His own number: 159 of 175 Y Combinator startups were enterprise.
content_html:
The Airbnb chief executive made the argument on the Yahoo Finance podcast Power Players with Brian Sozzi this week.

His diagnosis has two parts. “I think part of it’s a narrative issue that we’re not talking about AI correctly,” he said.

The second part is the product. “We need to actually be developing more products that just regular people can use.”

The number he chose implicates him

Chesky supplied the statistic himself, which is what makes it worth repeating. In Y Combinator’s most recent batch, 159 of 175 companies were enterprise rather than consumer.

He is on Y Combinator’s board. That does not make the observation wrong, and it does complicate the framing.

He put it as a loss of nerve. Compared with when he started Airbnb 18 years ago, founders now seem “afraid” to build for consumers, he said.

“Almost all AI is enterprise,” he added. “I think consumer is a huge gap.”

What he thinks has actually shipped

His assessment of the field is blunter than most people in it would risk. “There’s been very little progress on consumer AI,” he said. “ChatGPT is about what we’ve seen.”

He expects that to change within two to three years, in what he called a renaissance around consumer AI.

The example he reaches for is medical. AI could give somebody a doctor on demand who could not otherwise afford one, he argued.

That is the pitch, and it is worth noticing that it describes a product nobody has shipped.

The example also skips the hard part. Medical advice is regulated, and the obstacle to a doctor on demand is licensing and liability rather than model quality.

The thing he confirmed and then refused to discuss

Buried in the same conversation is a first. Chesky confirmed that Airbnb has an AI lab, which the company had never publicly acknowledged.

“I can confirm it exists, but I’m going to not say anything more about it right now,” he said.

Set that beside his complaint that the industry is not talking about AI correctly. He is right about the narrative problem, and he just demonstrated one version of it.

Airbnb wants to be the super app

The commercial plan behind the argument arrived in the same interview. Chesky said Airbnb is roughly a year to 18 months from becoming a fundamentally bigger service, adding rental cars and hotel rooms.

He framed the ambition honestly. Super apps exist in China, and he questioned openly whether one is possible in the US.

He also expects search to change first. Chatbots will handle destination discovery and itineraries before they handle reservations.

Airbnb will be “a completely different search paradigm”, he said.

Europe points the other way for the biggest platforms. The Digital Markets Act exists to prise bundles apart, although it applies to designated gatekeepers and Airbnb is not one of them.

That still shapes the ambition. A travel super app that worked would eventually be large enough to attract exactly that scrutiny.

The polling gives him his strongest point

This is where his case stops being a vibe. Pew Research found in June that 40% of US adults expect AI’s effect on society over the next 20 years to be negative.

Only 16% expect it to be positive. That is a two-to-one deficit on a technology the industry is spending hundreds of billions to build.

The response so far has mostly been communications. Several AI companies have run feel-good advertising, and chief executives keep publishing manifestos, including Mark Zuckerberg’s personal superintelligence essay this month.

Public patience with tech is thin more broadly. A recent poll found 61% of Americans favour stronger oversight of social media.

Some people are opting out in smaller ways. The desk has covered screen-fatigued workers reaching for pen and paper.

There is a duller reason enterprise won

Chesky calls it fear. The likelier explanation is arithmetic, and it deserves stating against him.

Enterprise buyers pay, sign multi-year contracts and tolerate rough software. Consumers churn, cost money to acquire, and expect the good version free.

An AI company burning cash on inference goes where the revenue is. That is not cowardice, it is the only survivable choice for most startups.

Airbnb’s own results make the point. AI customer service resolved 45% of inquiries last quarter and cut support costs per booking by 16%.

Those are cost-side wins, not consumer products. The most cited AI success at the company arguing for consumer AI is an internal efficiency number.

The counterexamples exist, including in Europe

The gap is real but it is not empty. Stockholm’s Lovable raised $400m at $13.3bn for a product that lets people build software by describing it in ordinary language.

That is closer to Chesky’s brief than most of what Silicon Valley shipped this year, and it came out of Europe.

Airbnb itself is the other answer. Its AI-native quarter produced $3.6bn of revenue, up 17%, with bookings up 10%.

So the company making the argument is also making money from it. That is a reason to take the argument seriously and to read it carefully.

The line that will get quoted

One claim from the interview will outrun everything else. “One person could be a billion-dollar company,” Chesky said. “I think we might’ve already seen that.”

He offered no example. He did say he codes personally, in Anthropic’s Claude Code, and that watching agents work is how he learns.

He also placed the moment historically. This is the fourth window in computing, he said, and bigger than the other three combined.

What would settle it

Two things, and the first is his own company. Airbnb has 12 to 18 months on the record for becoming something bigger than a rentals platform.

The second is the next Y Combinator batch. If the enterprise share falls meaningfully, the industry heard him. If it holds near 90%, founders are answering to their investors rather than to the polling.

Chesky is arguing that Silicon Valley should build things ordinary people want. The uncomfortable version of his own evidence is that it already knows what they want, and has decided it cannot make money selling it.

content_html_zh:
这位 Airbnb 首席执行官本周在雅虎财经播客 Power Players 中与布莱恩·索齐 (Brian Sozzi) 发表了这一论点。

他的诊断有两个部分。 “我认为部分原因在于我们没有正确谈论人工智能，”他说。

第二部分是产品。 “我们实际上需要开发更多普通人可以使用的产品。”

他选择的数字暗示了他

切斯基本人提供了该统计数据，因此值得重复。 在 Y Combinator 的最新批次中，175 家公司中有 159 家是企业而非消费者。

他是 Y Combinator 的董事会成员。 这并不意味着观察结果是错误的，而且确实使框架变得复杂。

他说这是失去勇气。 他说，与 18 年前创办 Airbnb 时相比，创始人现在似乎“害怕”为消费者打造服务。

“几乎所有人工智能都是企业级的，”他补充道。 “我认为消费者是一个巨大的差距。”

他所认为的实际上已发货

他对这个领域的评估比该领域的大多数人所冒的风险要直率。 “消费者人工智能方面进展甚微，”他说。 “ChatGPT 就是我们所看到的。”

他预计这种情况将在两到三年内发生改变，他称之为消费者人工智能的复兴。

他举的例子是医学上的。 他认为，人工智能可以为那些无法负担得起医生费用的人提供按需的医生服务。

这就是宣传语，值得注意的是，它描述了一种没有人发货的产品。

该示例还跳过了困难的部分。 医疗建议受到监管，按需医生的障碍是许可和责任，而不是模型质量。

他确认然后拒绝讨论的事情

埋藏在同一次谈话中的是第一次。 Chesky 证实 Airbnb 拥有一个人工智能实验室，但该公司从未公开承认过。

“我可以确认它的存在，但我现在不会再多说什么，”他说。

除此之外，他还抱怨业界没有正确谈论人工智能。 他对叙事问题的看法是正确的，而且他只是演示了其中的一个版本。

Airbnb 希望成为超级应用

争论背后的商业计划是在同一次采访中提出的。 切斯基表示，Airbnb 大约需要一年到 18 个月的时间才能成为一项规模更大的服务，增加汽车租赁和酒店房间。

他诚实地表达了自己的野心。 中国存在超级应用程序，他公开质疑美国是否有可能推出超级应用程序。

他还预计搜索将首先发生变化。 聊天机器人将在处理预订之前处理目的地发现和行程。

他表示，Airbnb 将成为“一个完全不同的搜索范式”。

欧洲为最大的平台指出了另一条路。 《数字市场法案》的存在是为了对捆绑包进行奖励，尽管它适用于指定的看门人，而 Airbnb 并不是其中之一。

这仍然塑造了我们的雄心。 一款行之有效的旅行超级应用程序最终将足够大，足以吸引这样的审查。

民意调查显示了他的最强点

这就是他的案子不再引起关注的地方。 皮尤研究中心 6 月发现，40% 的美国成年人预计人工智能在未来 20 年对社会的影响是负面的。

只有 16% 的人预计其结果是积极的。 对于该行业花费数千亿美元打造的技术来说，这是二比一的赤字。

迄今为止的回应主要是沟通。 几家人工智能公司已经投放了让人感觉良好的广告，首席执行官们不断发布宣言，包括马克·扎克伯格本月的个人超级智能文章。

从更广泛的角度来看，公众对科技的耐心很薄弱。 最近的一项民意调查发现，61% 的美国人赞成加强对社交媒体的监管。

有些人选择以较小的方式退出。 桌子上摆满了因屏幕而疲劳的工作人员，他们伸手拿笔和纸。

企业获胜有一个更乏味的理由

切斯基称之为恐惧。 更可能的解释是算术，并且值得对他进行反对。

企业买家付费、签署多年合同并容忍粗糙的软件。 消费者会流失，花钱购买，并期望免费获得好的版本。

人工智能公司在推理上烧钱的地方就是收入所在的地方。 这并不是怯懦，而是大多数初创公司唯一的生存选择。

Airbnb 自己的结果就说明了这一点。 人工智能客户服务上季度解决了 45% 的询问，并将每次预订的支持成本降低了 16%。

这些是成本方面的胜利，而不是消费产品。 在支持消费者人工智能的公司中，最常被提及的人工智能成功是内部效率数据。

反例是存在的，包括在欧洲

差距是真实存在的，但并不是空的。 斯德哥尔摩的 Lovable 筹集了 4 亿美元资金，融资额为 133 亿美元，其产品可以让人们通过用普通语言描述来构建软件。

这比硅谷今年发布的大部分产品更接近切斯基的简报，而且它来自欧洲。

Airbnb 本身就是另一个答案。 其 AI 原生季度收入达 36 亿美元，增长 17%，预订量增长 10%。

因此，提出论点的公司也从中赚钱。 这就是认真对待这个论点并仔细阅读它的原因。

将被引用的行

采访中的一项主张胜过其他一切。 “一个人可以成为一家价值十亿美元的公司，”切斯基说。 “我想我们可能已经看到了这一点。”

他没有提供任何例子。 他确实说过，他亲自编写代码，在 Anthropic 的克劳德代码中，观看代理工作就是他学习的方式。

他还将这一时刻置于历史地位。 他说，这是计算领域的第四个窗口，比其他三个窗口的总和还要大。

什么可以解决它

有两件事，第一是他自己的公司。 Airbnb 有 12 到 18 个月的时间才成为比租赁平台更大的平台。

第二个是下一个 Y Combinator 批次。 如果企业份额大幅下降，业界就会听到他的声音。 如果这一比例接近 90%，那么创始人就是在向投资者而不是民意调查做出回应。

切斯基认为硅谷应该建造普通人想要的东西。 他自己的证据令人不安的是，它已经知道他们想要什么，并决定出售它无法赚钱。
